description: Houston, We Have a Breakthrough is a team of three builders who believe the next giant leap in space exploration starts with effective problem solving.
summary: Choosing where to land on the Moon can make or break a mission; our app makes that decision faster and clearer. Built for NASA researchers, mission planners, and the general public, our tool brings official NASA data together in one dynamic application. An interactive 3D model of the Solar System gives users a heliocentric view of all major extraterrestrial bodies, while a dedicated Moon view evaluates and ranks potential landing sites based on multiple factors. Once a site is chosen, the app plans the route to reach it, including when the rocket should launch, when it will arrive, the fastest route and the most fuel efficient trajectory. It also shows which minerals can be found at each location, so users can weigh a site's scientific and resource value alongside its practicality. Time and speed controls allow users to observe motion in space while launched missions are being executed. Our customized AI advisor can guide users to solve challenging decisions and find resources. By combining site selection, mission timing, launch trajectory, and resource data in one place, our app turns complex lunar mission planning to create a scientific breakthrough in lunar landing site selection, even on unresearched southern terrain.
details:
L.U.N.A.R. (Lunar Unified Navigation Assistant & Reconnaissance) helps mission planners answer a question that decides whether a lunar south pole mission works: at a given site and date, will the lander have sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication, and for how long? At the south pole the Sun stays within about 1.5 degrees of the horizon, so a nearby hill can block it for days, and the horizon sits low enough that terrain can cut off radio contact. A few kilometers or a few days can change everything.

For each of 11 sites, our Python pipeline traces 360 directions across NASA's LOLA laser altimeter elevation map (60 m per pixel) out to 200 km, accounting for the Moon's curvature, to build the true terrain horizon. We combine this with hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons, covering August 2026 to October 2027, to determine hour by hour whether each site is sunlit and whether Earth is visible. A FastAPI backend turns this into the figures planners need: hours of sunlight remaining, time to loss of Earth contact, percentage of time illuminated, and every sunlight and communication window. A search ranks sites and landing dates against mission constraints, which directly supports the scenario in the challenge: when a launch slips, find a nearby site or date that still works. An AI advisor built from Anthropic's Claude lets users ask questions in plain language, but it can only request results from our own search and explain them, so every number shown comes from our calculations, never from the AI.

A CesiumJS 3D view shows the Earth-Moon system, historical missions and the selected site, and NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) runs live to compute an Earth-to-Moon transfer and lunar orbit capture, built on GMAT's own lunar transfer example. The converged solution uses a total burn of 746 m/s and 536 kg of propellant over a 5.05-day transfer.

We validated the science at each step. Our computed Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.004 degrees, the horizon calculation passes flat-Moon and ridge tests, and GMAT's propellant use matches the rocket equation exactly. The results also reproduce known features of the south pole: Malapert Massif keeps Earth in view at all times, while the permanently shadowed floor of Shackleton crater never sees the Sun.

NASA already has powerful tools such as QuickMap and Moon Trek, but they are slow for comparing many sites and dates. L.U.N.A.R. makes that comparison fast and understandable for mission planners, educators and the public. It also shows how much a small move matters: two points only 150 m apart on the Shackleton rim receive 86% and 22% sunlight.

We built L.U.N.A.R. with Python (NumPy, astroquery and FastAPI), JavaScript and CesiumJS, NASA GMAT, NASA LOLA elevation data, NASA JPL Horizons, CelesTrak, and Anthropic's Claude (Haiku).

Rather than building another map viewer, we compute the real terrain horizon at each site in seconds. We deliberately kept the AI as an explainer only, to avoid invented numbers, treated the 3D terrain as display only because it can differ from NASA altimeter data, and labelled every approximation. Our current limitations are that we use the centre of the Sun rather than the full disk, hourly time steps, a 60 m elevation map, and GMAT's fixed 2014 version; extending GMAT to any site and date is our next step.
